mcqs.question: In a successful CSRF attack, what does the attacker's page obtain?
options: The victim's session cookie, copied out of the browser
Read access to the victim's authenticated session data
Nothing readable — only the side effect of the state-changing request
A short-lived token it can replay from its own server
mcqs.explanation: The same-origin policy still blocks the attacker page from reading the response, so no credential or data is obtained — the damage is done purely by the request the server executed. Believing the cookie is stolen leads people to think HttpOnly or TLS would help, and neither is relevant here.

mcqs.question: An API authenticates with a bearer token that the SPA reads from memory and sets in an `Authorization` header. Why is this immune to CSRF?
options: A cross-site page can trigger the request but cannot read the token, so the request arrives unauthenticated
Bearer tokens are cryptographically bound to the originating page
The `Authorization` header is stripped by the browser on cross-site requests
CORS blocks the request from ever reaching the server
mcqs.explanation: CSRF depends on credentials the browser attaches automatically; a header the application sets explicitly requires reading the token, which the same-origin policy prevents, so the forged request simply gets a 401. CORS is not the reason — a preflight may be refused, but the underlying protection is that the credential never rides along.

mcqs.question: Your session cookie is `SameSite=Lax`. An attacker who has compromised `promo.yourapp.com` hosts an auto-submitting form targeting `app.yourapp.com`. Does SameSite stop it?
options: Yes — the cookie is only sent on requests initiated by the exact same origin
No — SameSite compares registrable domains, so the two subdomains are the same site
Yes — Lax blocks all cross-subdomain POST requests
No — but only because Lax permits POST requests generally
mcqs.explanation: SameSite operates on site, meaning the registrable domain, not on origin, so anything under yourapp.com is same-site and the cookie is attached normally. Lax does block genuinely cross-site POSTs — the gap here is subdomain scope, which is exactly why CSRF tokens remain necessary alongside SameSite.

mcqs.question: In the double-submit cookie pattern, why is it safe to put the CSRF token in a cookie that JavaScript can read?
options: Because the token is encrypted, so reading it reveals nothing useful
Because the cookie is marked HttpOnly and therefore unreadable by any script
Because a cross-site attacker can cause the cookie to be sent but cannot read it to build a matching header
Because the token changes on every request, so a copied value is already stale
mcqs.explanation: The attacker's page can make the browser attach cookies to a forged request, but the same-origin policy stops it reading them, so it cannot produce the matching header the server requires. The cookie deliberately is not HttpOnly here — your own JavaScript has to read it, which is the point of the pattern.

mcqs.question: A partner integration requires your session cookie on cross-site requests. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Set `SameSite=None` on the main session cookie and rely on CORS to restrict who can use it
Set `SameSite=None` without `Secure` so the cookie also works on the partner's HTTP pages
Refuse the integration, since cross-site cookies cannot be made safe
Issue a separate narrowly-scoped `SameSite=None; Secure` cookie for that surface and keep CSRF tokens mandatory everywhere
mcqs.explanation: Scoping the exception to its own limited cookie means only the embedded surface loses SameSite protection, and server-side tokens still cover every state-changing endpoint. Relaxing the main session cookie disables the defense product-wide, and CORS governs reading responses rather than whether forged requests are sent.
